blocks.text: Every program you will ever write does the same simple dance. It takes some input, does a little thinking, and produces some output. Learn those two and you can already build real, useful programs.

blocks.alt: How a program works: reads input, produces output

blocks.text: Input is any information you give the program: a number you type, a name, a file, a click. Output is anything the program shows back: text on the screen, a result, a saved file.
Every app you use is just input and output wrapped around some logic. You type a message (input), the app shows it to your friend (output). Master these two and everything else builds on top.
In this lesson we go slow and cover printing, reading input, converting text into numbers, formatting your output, reading many values, and the mistakes that trip up almost every beginner.
Printing is how your program talks back to you. It is almost always the very first thing you learn, and you will use it constantly to see what your code is doing.
Here is the famous first line of code in three popular languages:
Text inside quotation marks is printed exactly as written. Each of these prints the message and then moves to a new line, so whatever you print next starts fresh below.
Same Line or New Line
By default, most print commands move to a new line after printing. Sometimes you want several things on one line instead. Every language has a way to control this.

codes.python:
print("Hello", end=" ")   # stay on the same line, add a space
print("World")            # prints: Hello World
codes.java:
System.out.print("Hello ");   // print, no new line
System.out.println("World");  // println adds a new line

blocks.text: In Python, print normally ends with a new line, and you change that with the end setting. In Java, print stays on the line while println moves to the next.
When your output looks squashed together or spread across too many lines, the fix is almost always about new lines. Learn how your language starts a new line and you control the layout.
You will rarely print only fixed text. Usually you want to print the value of a variable, or mix text and values together.

codes.python:
score = 42
print("Your score is", score)     # Your score is 42
codes.java:
int score = 42;
System.out.println("Your score is " + score);
codes.cpp:
int score = 42;
cout << "Your score is " << score << endl;

blocks.text: The clean way in Python
Python has a lovely feature called an f string that lets you drop values right inside the text. It keeps things readable when you combine several values.

codes.python:
name = "Riya"
score = 42
print(f"{name} scored {score} points")   # Riya scored 42 points

blocks.text: Combining text and values is something you will do in almost every program. Pick the style your language prefers and it becomes second nature quickly.
Formatting Numbers in Output
Sometimes a raw number looks messy, like a price showing as 3.9999999. You often want to control how many decimals appear.

codes.python:
pi = 3.14159265
print(round(pi, 2))         # 3.14
print(f"{pi:.2f}")          # 3.14, formatted to two decimals

blocks.text: Rounding to a fixed number of decimals is common for money, averages, and measurements. Learn the way your language does it, because messy numbers make output look unprofessional.
There is a difference between rounding a value for display and changing the value itself. Formatting for output does not change the number stored in your variable.
Reading input lets the user type something and your program respond to it. This is what makes a program interactive instead of fixed.
Be careful here, because it catches almost every beginner: input almost always arrives as text, even if the user typed a number.

codes.python:
name = input()              # read one line of text
print("Hello,", name)

blocks.text: In each case, the program pauses, waits for the user to type and press enter, and then stores what they typed so you can use it.
Reading Numbers
This is the number one beginner trap, so we will slow right down. Since input comes in as text, the characters "5" are not the same as the number 5. You cannot do math on text.
Before you can add, subtract, or compare, you must convert the text into a real number.

codes.python:
n = int(input())     # turn the text "5" into the number 5
print(n * 2)         # now math works, prints 10

blocks.text: What happens if you forget to convert
If you skip the conversion in Python and try to do math, you get a surprising result. For example, the text "5" times 2 gives "55", because it repeats the text instead of adding.
If your math gives a strange result or an error, the very first thing to check is whether you forgot to convert the input from text into a number. This one bug costs beginners hours.
Whole numbers are not the only kind. When you need numbers with a decimal point, like a price or an average, you convert to a floating point number instead.
The idea is the same as reading whole numbers. You just use the decimal type instead of the integer type.
Reading Multiple Values
Often you need two or more values, sometimes typed on the same line separated by spaces. Here is how to read two numbers and add them together.

codes.python:
a, b = map(int, input().split())   # "3 4" becomes a = 3 and b = 4
print(a + b)                        # 7

blocks.text: Reading a whole list of numbers
Sometimes the input is a line with many numbers. In Python you can read them all into a list in one clean line.
The pattern is always the same: read the line, split it into pieces, and convert each piece to a number. Once you see it once, you will reuse it in almost every problem.

content.title: 5. Reading a Fixed Number of Lines

blocks.text: Many problems start by telling you how many items follow. You read that count first, then loop that many times to read the rest.

codes.python:
n = int(input())          # how many numbers follow
nums = []
for _ in range(n):
    nums.append(int(input()))
print(sum(nums))

blocks.text: This is an extremely common shape in DSA problems: first a count, then that many lines or values. Recognising it makes reading input effortless.

content.title: 6. A Full Example, Start to Finish

blocks.text: Let us put it all together in one small program. It reads two numbers and prints their sum, difference, and product. This is the shape of countless beginner programs.

codes.python:
a, b = map(int, input().split())

print("Sum:", a + b)
print("Difference:", a - b)
print("Product:", a * b)

blocks.text: Read the input, do the work, print the output. That simple three step shape, read then process then print, is the skeleton of almost every program you will write for a long time.
Sometimes you do not know in advance how many values are coming. The input simply keeps going until it ends. In that case you read in a loop until there is nothing left.

codes.python:
import sys
for line in sys.stdin:          # keep reading every line until the input ends
    line = line.strip()
    if line:
        print("Got:", line)

blocks.text: This is common when a problem says something like "read numbers until end of file". The loop stops automatically when the input runs out.
If your program seems to hang forever waiting for input, you may be reading in an endless loop with no natural end. Make sure your loop can actually stop.
Many practice problems give you several test cases in one run. The input starts with a number telling you how many cases follow, and you print one answer per case.

codes.python:
cases = int(input())         # how many test cases
for _ in range(cases):
    a, b = map(int, input().split())
    print(a + b)             # one line of output per case

blocks.text: This shape, a count followed by that many cases, is everywhere in DSA practice. Recognising it makes these problems feel routine.
For most problems, the normal way of reading and printing is perfectly fine. But when the input is huge, say a million numbers, the normal way can become slow enough to fail a tight time limit.
Each language offers a faster path for these cases.

items: Python: read everything at once with sys.stdin instead of many input calls.
Java: use BufferedReader instead of Scanner for large inputs.
C++: turn off the sync with C streams and untie cin from cout.

codes.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()   # read all input at once, then process

blocks.text: Do not reach for fast input and output until you actually hit a time limit. For learning and normal problems, the simple way is clearer and good enough.
The humble print statement is your best friend when something goes wrong. When your program misbehaves, sprinkle prints to see the actual values at each step.

codes.python:
n = int(input())
print("DEBUG: n is", n)     # check what you actually read
result = n * 2
print("DEBUG: result is", result)

items: Print the raw input to confirm you read what you expected.
Print values before the line that breaks to see the real state.
Label your debug prints so you can tell them apart.

blocks.text: Remember to remove your debug prints before submitting to a judge, or they will count as wrong output. Keep them while learning, clean them before you finish.
Once you start working with lists of data, you will want to print them neatly. Printing a whole list directly often looks messy, so you usually join the values into a clean line.

codes.python:
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print(nums)                       # [5, 2, 9, 1], includes brackets
print(*nums)                      # 5 2 9 1, values separated by spaces
print(", ".join(map(str, nums)))  # 5, 2, 9, 1, joined by commas

blocks.text: Choosing how to join the values, by spaces or commas, lets you match whatever output format a problem asks for.
Many problems are marked wrong only because the output format is slightly off. Read the required format carefully and match it exactly.
Most early bugs come from this short list, so keep it close.

items: Doing math on input without converting it from text to a number first
Forgetting that printing usually adds a new line every time
Reading a single value when the input actually contains several
Reading values in a different order than they were given
Trying to convert text that is not a number, which causes an error
Mixing up reading a whole line versus reading one word or number

blocks.text: When something goes wrong with input and output, slow down and print the raw value you read. Seeing exactly what your program received usually reveals the bug in seconds.
Why does my number act like text?
Because input arrives as text by default. You must convert it with something like int or float before doing math.
How do I print without moving to a new line?
Use your language setting for it, such as the end option in Python or print instead of println in Java.
How do I read several numbers on one line?
Read the whole line, split it on spaces, and convert each piece to a number. In Python this is one line with split and map.
Why does my output have too many decimals?
That is the raw value. Round it or format it to the number of decimals you want when you print.

items: Input: information you give the program.
Output: what the program shows back.
Convert or cast: change a value from one type to another, such as text to a number.
Concatenate: join pieces of text together.
Format: control how a value looks when printed, such as decimals.

blocks.text: The only way to make this automatic is to write small programs. Try these.

items: Read your name and print a greeting.
Read two numbers and print their sum, difference, and product.
Read three numbers and print their average, rounded to two decimals.
Read a temperature in Celsius and print it in Fahrenheit.
Read a count, then that many numbers, and print the largest one.

blocks.text: Once printing and reading feel natural, you are ready to store and reuse values with confidence. That is exactly what variables are for, and it is the next lesson.
